dimensions.name: Spec decoding & S3/SigV4 fidelity research

evidence.note: Opening is pure environment recon (ls, python version, pip list); no attempt to catalog required operations, the error/status matrix, auth modes, or SigV4 rules before coding.
Agent writes the entire main.py from memory in successive append-blocks with no spec inventory or SigV4 research phase — codes the auth/canonicalization core blind.

SigV4 canonicalization defects (parse_qs reorder/decode, raw query string needed, double-encoding, safe='-_.~', payload hash from x-amz-content-sha256) are discovered only via boto3 SignatureDoesNotMatch failures and patched iteratively — reactive discovery, not proactive grounding; no capture of real boto3 signed requests.
boto3 XML namespace quirk in CompleteMultipartUpload found only when the test errors 'InvalidPart', confirming gaps surface through test failure rather than research.
Discovers boto3 sends dict (not XML strings) for CORS/lifecycle/notification config only at test time, again a spec/behavior gap found reactively.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent skimmed the spec and coded the whole service — including the SigV4 auth core — from memory, treating canonicalization and boto3 quirks as things to guess at and discovering every gap (query-string canonicalization, double-encoding, content-sha256 payload hash, XML namespaces, config dict-vs-XML) only when boto3 tests failed. That is squarely anchor 3. It stops short of 5 because the hard parts were never researched or validated against ground truth before implementation, and it never built a durable reference or captured real signed requests; the correct mechanisms it eventually reached were arrived at purely through test-failure debugging.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Built main.py in a deliberate section-by-section order that reflects a sensible dependency chain: constants/XML utils → storage helpers → SigV4 auth → audit/notification → policy eval → S3 routes → multipart/config handlers → admin API → lifecycle worker. Foundational auth/storage substrate was written before dependent features, and each 'Plan:' names the next discrete subsystem.

Verified basic signed CRUD (ListBuckets/CreateBucket/PutObject/GetObject) and then SigV4 rejection of bad credentials as an implicit gate before moving on to multipart/advanced features — an emergent 'done-check' per foundational milestone rather than a pre-declared acceptance criterion.

Testing proceeded in layered order — basic CRUD → multipart complete → versioning/tagging → presigned → admin API → console API → bucket configs → cross-tenant/quota — treating each subsystem as a discrete checkable unit, but the ordering was driven reactively by test results, not a stated milestone plan.

Closing checklist enumerates implemented subsystems with ✓ marks, showing the subsystem list was tracked; but this is a retrospective inventory, not an up-front milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance criteria or the two grading surfaces scoped as separate tracks.

Long stretch of SigV4 query-string debugging where the same multi-item to-do ('fix dispatch, add locks, fix lifespan, fix payload hash…') is restated across many steps as a flat running list rather than a structured, risk-ordered milestone map — no explicit re-partitioning of the plan.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a clear, reasonable dependency order — foundational SigV4 auth and storage substrate first, dependent features (multipart, versioning, configs, admin, console) layered after — and treated each subsystem as a discrete unit, matching the level-5 anchor. There is some emergent 'done-checking' (basic signed PUT/GET and auth rejection proven before multipart), nudging above a flat to-do list, but it falls short of level 8: milestones were never laid out as an explicit hierarchy with stated per-milestone acceptance checks, the two grading surfaces were not scoped as separate tracks, and the mid-trajectory planning devolved into a repeatedly-restated flat list rather than a re-partitioned, risk-ordered map.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & the DOM contract

evidence.note: Real boto3 round-trips for core CRUD and deliberate wrong-credential SigV4 probes (SignatureDoesNotMatch vs InvalidAccessKeyId), catching real breakage — well beyond ad hoc pokes.
boto3 edge-case verification: multipart complete with ETag format check, versioning, tagging, CopyObject, multi-object delete — systematic per-operation exercising.

Admin API and console API tested directly via curl; presigned GET/PUT, ranged 206, invalid range 416, conditional 304, cross-tenant 403 all confirmed with boto3/HTTP — hits multiple grader conditions.
Console verified only by static grep of data-testids in app.js and 200-status static file loads; no browser DOM/side-effect verification.

Concurrency (30-client), lifecycle fast-clock expiry, notification webhook delivery/retry, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and audit atomicity were named as 'still need to verify' but never actually executed before submit — subsystems left unverified.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it used real boto3 to exercise not just main operations but many edge cases (multipart ETag, ranged 206/416, conditional 304, cross-tenant status codes) and hit admin/console APIs directly, using failures to drive fixes. But it falls short of level 8 because two of that anchor's three pillars are missing: no concurrency stress test for the explicit 30-client requirement (only lock code was added), and console verification was a static testid grep rather than browser side-effect checks. Lifecycle, notification, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and audit-atomicity were acknowledged but never run, so no reusable regression harness exists — placing it solidly between 5 and 8.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across subsystems

evidence.note: Running prose checklists enumerating which operations work vs remain (multipart create works/complete fails, tagging PUT works/GET empty, versioning works), and recognizing partially-done subsystems.

Cross-checks console data-testids extracted from app.js against the spec's enumerated list, catching loading-indicator missing as a testid element and fixing it — coverage checked against enumerated surface.

~20-step circular struggle on SigV4 canonical-query-string canonicalization; repeated failed replacements. Recognition of the stuck state and redirect (full rewrite) only comes ~step 74-76, i.e. late rather than early.

Final comprehensive ✅ checklist per operation and error code; however lifecycle/notification workers flagged as 'still need to verify' at step 110 are claimed complete at submission without clear verification — a coverage-map overstatement.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained granular, roughly accurate coverage tracking down to individual operations, error codes, and console testids (steps 44, 90, 116), and cross-checked testids against the spec's enumerated surface (step 110-114), which exceeds the level-5 'running checklist' anchor and reaches into level 8 with explicit partial-subsystem recognition and eventual circular-debugging recognition. It is held below 8/10 because the tracking was re-derived in prose rather than a maintained artifact, the SigV4 thrashing ran ~20 steps before the stuck state was recognized and redirected, and the final coverage picture asserted completeness on lifecycle/notification subsystems it had earlier flagged as unverified. This places it at a 7.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: CreateBucket returned 404 and wrong-secret returned AccessDenied instead of SignatureDoesNotMatch. Agent diagnosed the true root cause both times: dispatch checked bucket existence before determining operation type, and the dispatch rewrite took resolve_tenant()[0] and silently dropped the auth-error response. Fixed the design (reorder dispatch, propagate errors) rather than patching symptoms.

Repeated SignatureDoesNotMatch on multipart/ListObjectsV2 (query-param requests). Agent isolated the exact canonicalization divergence — parse_qs reorders/decodes query params, so it must use the raw query string — then caught a follow-on double-encoding bug (raw query already percent-encoded) and corrected build_canonical_query_string to decode-then-reencode with correct safe chars. Textbook root-cause isolation of a SigV4 step, sustained through many hard mismatches.

CompleteMultipartUpload InvalidPart: diagnosed boto3 sends namespaced XML that findall('Part') can't match. Rather than fix only that call, propagated namespace-aware parsing (findall_ns/find_ns shared helpers) across ALL XML subsystems — DeleteObjects, notification, lifecycle, tagging — then grepped to verify no bare .find/.findall remained, closing the whole class of error. This is cross-subsystem propagation + verification, the top-anchor behavior.

Correctly distinguished test-harness bugs from implementation bugs: recognized the ranged-GET failure was the test using resp['StatusCode'] (server actually returned 206 per logs), and that CORS/lifecycle/notification failures were because boto3 expects dicts not XML strings, so switched to raw curl/XML verification instead of 'fixing' correct code.

Countervailing: several rounds where sed/python replacements silently failed to match, and the agent re-attempted essentially the same edit before noticing 'the replacement didn't take effect because the old block wasn't matched' and switching to read-exact-then-rewrite. Some churn on edit mechanics, though it did eventually self-correct the approach.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently treated failures as signal, diagnosing to root cause (SigV4 parse_qs vs raw query, error-propagation drop, XML namespaces) with evidence rather than random tweaks, matching anchor 8. It exceeded a plain 8 by propagating the namespace fix across every affected XML subsystem via shared helpers and verifying with grep that the class was fully closed, and by correctly attributing several failures to the test harness rather than the code — behaviors from anchor 10. It falls short of a full 10 because of repeated churn on silently-failing edits (steps 63-77) and limited systematic updating of the plan/verification beyond the namespace case, so I place the observed level at 8.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across the split grader

evidence.note: Console UI (index.html, app.js, styles.css) built in a single early pass with all required views/testids; step 16 notes it is 'crucial for the browser-based grading', showing both surfaces were acknowledged and the console was not left a stub.

The vast majority of the trajectory is iterative data-plane/SigV4 debugging (query-string canonicalization, multipart XML namespaces, tagging, presigned URLs). Effort was heavily skewed toward correctness-stage perfection.

Console only lightly revisited: curl confirms it loads (200), grep verifies data-testids present, and the missing loading-indicator testid is added. No browser-based verification of UX side-effects (modal-once secret, confirm dialog, empty-state) — a shallow pass on the half-score surface.
Final self-summary enumerates data-plane features in exhaustive detail with the console mentioned only briefly; no explicit reasoning about the 50/50 weighting or pacing between surfaces.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent allocated real effort to both surfaces — it built a complete console with all required testids/views/modals (not a stub) and heavily worked the data plane — matching anchor 5. However, it never explicitly reasoned about the 50/50 split or deliberately paced work across the two surfaces, and its console attention was a one-shot build plus shallow static checks (testid grep, load confirmation, one added testid) rather than verifying the browser-graded UX behaviors, so it falls short of anchor 8.

rubric.task_read: This is an extremely large, long-horizon build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store spanning SigV4 auth (byte-exact against boto3), a broad data plane (multipart, versioning, ranged reads, conditional ops, policies, notifications, lifecycle), an admin JSON API, an audit log, a background lifecycle worker, concurrency guarantees, and a browser-verified web console with a precise DOM contract. Difficulty comes from breadth (many loosely-coupled subsystems), unforgiving exactness (SigV4 signatures, pinned ETag/error semantics, load-bearing data-testids), and a split grader (binary correctness stage + UX rubric worth half). A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in orientation, sequencing, self-built verification, and progress tracking — over-investment is hard to reach here; the risk is thrash and lost threads.

dimensions.name: Spec decoding & S3/SigV4 fidelity research
dimensions.description: Extracting the exact contract from a dense spec and grounding the AWS-compatible behaviors (SigV4 canonicalization, pinned ETag/error/status semantics, boto3 quirks) before and while coding.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The correctness stage is binary and byte-exact against boto3; a misread of SigV4 rules, the multipart ETag formula, presigned/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD handling, or the cross-tenant status matrix silently fails whole test families. Blind coding here is fatal.

anchors.0: Starts implementing endpoints with no attempt to catalog the spec's requirements or understand SigV4/boto3 behavior.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes from memory; treats SigV4 and the error/status matrix as things to guess at, discovering gaps only when tests fail.
anchors.5: Enumerates the required operations and error codes, and correctly researches the core hard parts (SigV4 canonical request/signing, path-style routing) before implementing them.
anchors.8: Systematically inventories the full contract (auth modes, pinned ETag/range/error semantics, tenant status matrix, console DOM testids, admin schemas) and probes real boto3 behavior to nail canonicalization edge cases (UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, query-signing, clock skew) rather than assuming.
anchors.10: Builds a durable reference of the exact contract and continuously validates ambiguous behaviors against ground truth (e.g. capturing real boto3 signed requests, confirming header casing/encoding), resolving under-specified corners with evidence and revisiting them as new subsystems expose new interactions.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking the build into an ordered hierarchy of independently-checkable subsystems (auth core → bucket/object CRUD → multipart/versioning → policies/notifications/lifecycle → admin/audit → console) with a defensible dependency order.
dimensions.why_it_matters: There are ~10 loosely-coupled subsystems plus two grading surfaces. Without milestone structure and a sane order (auth and storage substrate first, since everything depends on them), the agent risks half-finishing many pieces and passing none of the binary stage.

anchors.0: No decomposition; codes in an undifferentiated stream with no notion of stages or completion criteria.
anchors.3: A vague or flat to-do list that mixes trivial and load-bearing items, with no dependency ordering and no per-item definition of done.
anchors.5: Clear list of the major subsystems tackled in a reasonable order (foundational auth/storage before dependent features), each treated as a discrete unit.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with correct dependency sequencing and a stated 'done' check per milestone (e.g. 'boto3 can PUT/GET a signed object' before layering multipart), and the two grading surfaces scoped as separate tracks.
anchors.10: Milestones are risk-ordered so the highest-uncertainty foundations (SigV4 exactness, concurrent storage substrate) are proven earliest, each with a concrete acceptance check, and the plan is re-partitioned as reality reveals coupling — sustaining a coherent map across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & the DOM contract
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, curl/HTTP probes, concurrency stress, console DOM/testid checks — beyond the hidden grader, rather than assuming code works.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is binary and hidden; the console is browser-verified against exact data-testids. The only way to know a subsystem passes is to reproduce the grader's conditions locally. Unverified subsystems are effectively untested until they silently fail.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because they were written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual pokes at a couple of endpoints; no boto3 round-trip, no concurrency check, no console DOM verification.
anchors.5: Uses real boto3 to exercise the main data-plane operations and hits the admin/console APIs directly, catching obvious breakage.
anchors.8: Systematic verification per subsystem: boto3 round-trips for edge cases (multipart ETag, ranged 206/416, conditional/precondition, cross-tenant status codes), a concurrency test for the 30-client requirement, and console checks that assert the required testids and side-effects.
anchors.10: Builds a reusable verification harness that mirrors grader conditions across all subsystems (including presigned/UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD signing, notification webhook delivery/retry, lifecycle expiry with the fast-clock env var, audit-line atomicity under concurrency), runs it repeatedly to catch regressions, and treats a subsystem as done only when its checks are green.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across subsystems
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which of the many subsystems/operations/error-codes are done, in progress, or untouched, and detecting stalls or circular debugging.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of operations and error codes across two grading surfaces over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot — believing the build is near-complete while whole families (e.g. notifications, lifecycle, a console view) are missing or half-done.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done vs remaining; repeatedly rediscovers or re-touches the same areas.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; loses track of which error codes/operations remain and drifts between areas without closure.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystems/operations and marks them off as completed, giving a roughly accurate done-vs-remaining view.
anchors.8: Granular, maintained tracking down to individual operations, error codes, and console testids, with explicit recognition when a subsystem is only partially done and when a debugging effort is going in circles.
anchors.10: Sustains an accurate coverage map across the entire horizon, cross-checked against the spec's enumerated surface (every error code, every notification event, every admin route, every testid), and reliably surfaces stuck/thrashing states early enough to redirect effort instead of grinding.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising approach when a verification fails or a boto3/SigV4 assumption is disproven, rather than repeatedly patching a broken model.
dimensions.why_it_matters: SigV4 and byte-exact behaviors are notorious for subtle mismatches; the agent will hit failing signatures and mismatched status codes. Progress depends on diagnosing the true cause and revising, not re-trying superficial fixes on a wrong mental model.

anchors.0: Ignores failures or keeps making the same change; barrels ahead on assumptions already shown false.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures with random tweaks and no root-cause reasoning; abandons hard subsystems instead of correcting course.
anchors.5: When a check fails, investigates the cause and makes a targeted fix, adjusting the approach for that subsystem.
anchors.8: Diagnoses failures to root cause (e.g. isolating exactly which SigV4 canonicalization step diverges from boto3), and revises the design or shared abstractions when a foundational assumption proves wrong.
anchors.10: Treats divergence as signal: pinpoints root causes with evidence, propagates the correction across all affected subsystems (not just the failing case), and updates the plan/verification so the same class of error can't recur — sustaining forward progress through repeated hard mismatches.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across the split grader
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary correctness stage and the browser-verified console UX rubric, which each contribute half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The console UX is worth half the score yet is easy to under-serve while sinking unbounded time into SigV4/data-plane perfection; conversely, a polished console with a broken data plane also caps the score. Explicit allocation across the two surfaces is a task-specific meta-decision beyond generic sequencing.

anchors.0: Pours all effort into one surface (e.g. the data plane) and never meaningfully addresses the other.
anchors.3: Acknowledges both surfaces but lets one consume nearly all effort with no deliberate balancing.
anchors.5: Allocates real effort to both the correctness stage and the console, ensuring neither is left as a stub.
anchors.8: Explicitly reasons about the 50/50 weighting and paces work so both surfaces reach a passing bar, defending the console's required views/testids and side-effects while securing core data-plane correctness.
anchors.10: Actively manages the effort budget across the horizon against the split grader — securing must-pass foundations on both surfaces first, then investing marginal effort where it yields the most score, and revisiting the balance as each surface's state becomes clear.
